Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 166 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2021) 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit 166 (WMU 166), Sullivan Lake, covers an area of 4,206 km2. The WMU contains 
portions of the central parkland and northern fescue natural subregions, and transition zone between subregions. 
The WMU is primarily deeded land, with limited Crown parcels, and has significant agricultural development in the 
south and eastern portions of the WMU. There are remaining large tracts of aspen parkland in the Rumsey Natural 
Area, Rumsey Ecological reserve, and private lands in the central parkland portion of the WMU. 
A survey for ungulates (mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose) was last conducted for WMU 166 in 2014 using 
the same strip-transect methodology, so results between 2014 and 2021 are directly comparable although the 
2014 survey occurred after antler-drop for deer. See Table 1 for previous ungulate survey estimates for WMU 166. 
The objective of the February 2021 survey was to assess the status of ungulate populations in WMU 166 by 
determining estimates for abundance, density and age-sex composition. We also recorded observations of 
additional species of game management or conservation concern including carnivores, game birds,  and sensitive 
or At Risk species. 
Survey Method 
The transect survey was conducted flying 48 east-west lines at 1.6 km intervals, with 37% coverage (600 m wide 
survey strip, area surveyed 1,569 km2) from February 1-3, 2021 with a total linear survey effort of 2,615 km. At 
each observation point, ungulates were classified by species, and when possible, sex and age were recorded.  
Antler size for deer was classified as ‘small’ (spike or two points on one or both antlers), ‘medium’ (antlers with 3 or 
more points; antlers inside ears) or large (antlers with ≥ 4 points, antlers outside of ears). Antler drop in mule deer 
and white-tailed deer was observed with several one-antlered bucks, so buck:doe, and therefore doe:fawn ratios 
are conservative estimates. 
 
Density was  calculated for white-tailed deer, mule deer and moose following Jolly 1969 (as described in Krebs 
2014) for surveys conducted with unequal sized units without replacement because the transect lengths varied. 
Density was multiplied by the WMU area to determine population estimates. 90% confidence intervals were also 
calculated. Although correction factor for deer detection can be applied in parkland regions (e.g. Habib et al. 2012), 
results reported are as observed, and likely to be conservative estimates of white-tailed and mule deer abundance. 
 
Elk observations were recorded during the survey, but population estimates were not calculated because the 
design of this survey is not appropriate for elk population calculation. Minimum total count of elk is reported. 
 
Results 
A total of 731 white-tailed deer were observed with an average group size of 5.0 (range 1-34)  . The estimated 
density was 0.46 deer/km2 and the estimated abundance was 1,959 individuals (90% CI 1,724 – 2,196), 
representing a 40% decline in white-tailed deer abundance since the last transect survey in 2014. A total of 649 
white-tailed deer were classified with a buck:doe:fawn ratio of 34:100:77. That results in an estimated 2021 winter 
white-tailed deer population of 313 buck, 921 doe, and 705 fawn. Of the 104 white-tailed deer bucks classified, 
46% were ‘small’, 37% ‘medium’, and 17% ‘large’. 
 
A total of 1,374 mule deer were observed with an average group size of 7.1 (range 1-33). The estimated density 
was 0.88 mule deer/km2 and the estimated abundance was 3,683 individuals (90% CI 3,153 – 4,213), representing

a 59% increase in mule deer abundance since the last transect survey in 2014. A total of 1,434 mule deer were 
classified with a buck:doe:fawn ratio of 52:100:81. That results in an estimated 2021 winter mule deer population of  
810 buck, 1,584 doe, and 1,289 fawn. Of the 261 mule deer bucks classified, 31% were ‘small’, 43% ‘medium’, and 
26% ‘large’. 
 
A total of 278 moose were observed with an average group size of 2.1 (range 1-9). The estimated density was 
0.18 moose/km2 and the estimated abundance was 745 individuals (90% CI 658 – 833), representing a 17% 
increase in moose abundance since the last transect survey in 2014. A total of 248 moose were classified with 
roughly equal representation of each age/sex class (84 bull, 83 cow, 81 calf) or a bull:cow:calf ratio of 100:100:97. 
That results in an estimated 2021 winter moose population of 253 bull, 253 cow, and 246 calf. 
 
A total of 244 elk were observed with group size ranging from 2-73. Of the 207 elk classified, 54 were bull, 98 cow, 
and 55 calf for a bull:cow:calf ratio of 55:100:56. Minimum total count of elk has continued to increase from 18 in 
2006 and 103 in 2014. 
 
We also observed 121 coyotes, 97 sharp-tailed grouse, five gray partridge, two red fox, two bald eagle, two snowy 
owl, and one great blue heron colony.These are incidental observations only and should not be considered 
minimum total counts.
